title: Looking inside a raw camera image

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A photo from your phone is polished. A raw image straight off a camera sensor is the unpolished data underneath. RawAnalyser is a Python tool that lets Antoine look right into it.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Three main things. Black and white clipping, meaning whether the darkest and brightest values are cut off. Gamma. And flatness, including vignette detection, which is how much the image darkens toward the corners. The vignette idea comes from Algolux.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: How do you tell it where to look?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: With a small JSON file that marks the region of interest and the gray patches, those neutral squares used for measuring. You give the script a folder of raw images plus that file, and choose which analyses to run: clipping, gamma, vignette or histograms.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Drawing coordinates by hand sounds painful.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's what the GUI is for. It lets you select the region and gray patches on a raw or TIFF file, saves them to the JSON file, and keeps watching the folder for new images as they arrive.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes, a small script called RawPixel. Give it a file and coordinates, and it tells you the pixel's value and its color according to the Bayer pattern, the checkerboard of red, green and blue filters on a sensor. There's also a helper that converts twenty megapixel images to five for a particular sensor.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Is there an example of the sensor info?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The page shows one: an OV2740 camera, ten-bit sensor values, and a B G G R Bayer pattern. The GitHub repository has all the options and usage examples.
